title: A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang
subtitle: Yang Xuanzhi · Northern Wei Luoyang · The Rise-and-Fall Epic of 1,367 Buddhist Temples
description: Yang Xuanzhi, a native of Beiping of the Northern Wei with little known of his life. In the fifth year of the Eastern Wei Wuding reign (547), he revisited Luoyang and witnessed the desolation of its Buddhist temples after the Northern Wei capital had been moved to Yecheng. Recalling the former splendor, he wrote the five-volume A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang, documenting the founding origins, architectural scale, and human stories of 1,367 Buddhist temples in the Northern Wei capital. It is the finest historical record of a city's temples in ancient China. This route follows the famous monastery sites that once made Luoyang a Buddhist holy land.

route.title: A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang: The Glory and Ruins of 1,367 Northern Wei Temples
route.intro:
Within and beyond the capital, there were over a thousand temples. Today the grounds are desolate, their bells rarely heard.
Yang Xuanzhi lived in an age when the Northern Wei was turning from prosperity to decline. In the eighteenth year of the Taihe reign (494), Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang and vigorously promoted Buddhism. Buddhist temples sprang up like bamboo shoots after rain—at their peak, they numbered 1,367. Every morning, a thousand copper bells rang in unison, and the entire city of Luoyang was enveloped in the sound of Sanskrit chanting. But only forty-odd years later, the Northern Wei split apart, the Eastern Wei moved its capital to Yecheng, and Luoyang was reduced to ruin. In the fifth year of the Wuding reign (547), Yang Xuanzhi returned to Luoyang on official business. Walking on streets overgrown with weeds, seeing the once-golden temples mostly collapsed, the bells silent, he felt a flood of emotion. He took up his brush and wrote this Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang. He was not simply being nostalgic—he used each temple as a coordinate to weave a city map of Northern Wei Luoyang. Behind every pagoda and every wall were living people and their stories. Let us follow Yang Xuanzhi's steps into that Luoyang of Buddha light, which ultimately returned to dust.

stops.title: Stop One: Yongning Temple—The Tallest Wooden Pagoda in Chinese History
stops.content: The first temple in the first volume of A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang is Yongning Temple. Yang Xuanzhi gave it his most intense ink, for it was the symbol of Northern Wei Luoyang—the Yongning Temple Pagoda, nine stories high, "visible from a hundred li outside the capital," was the tallest wooden structure in Chinese history, bar none. According to Yang Xuanzhi, the pagoda was built by the devout Empress Dowager Ling (Hu) in the first year of the Xiping reign (516). It was a wooden structure, nine stories, with flying eaves and golden bells on each level. "On windy nights, the jeweled bells chimed in harmony, their crisp ring audible for over ten miles." When Bodhidharma arrived in Luoyang and saw this pagoda, he "chanted hymns and praised it, pressing his palms together for days on end." Yet this miracle of a pagoda stood for only eighteen years—in the third year of the Yongxi reign (534), lightning struck, igniting a fire "that burned for three months without going out." Even a thousand years later, reading this still makes one sigh in despair. The Yongning Temple site now lies fifteen kilometers east of Luoyang, with only an earthen platform remaining—the base of that thousand-foot pagoda. Archaeological excavations have unearthed a large number of exquisite clay Buddha fragments, confirming that Yang Xuanzhi's account was true in every word. Standing on the weed-covered site, close your eyes—you can almost hear the wind bells that rang "audible for over ten miles" 1,500 years ago. Yang Xuanzhi's description of the Yongning Temple Pagoda is among the finest examples of ancient Chinese architectural writing. He wrote that the spire held a "golden jeweled vase, holding twenty-five hu," beneath which were "thirty tiers of dew-collecting golden plates, each hung with golden bells." Golden bells also hung from each of the four corners on every story, each as large as a stone jar. On windy nights, "the jeweled bells chimed in harmony, their crisp ring audible for over ten miles." This technique of describing architecture through sound makes the reader feel as if they are not reading words but listening to a symphony crossing a thousand years. Even more valuable, Yang Xuanzhi recorded construction details—"the pagoda has four sides, each with three doors and six windows, all lacquered vermilion. On each door are five rows of golden nails"—precise down to the number and color of the doors, even counting the golden nails, providing invaluable primary data for today's archaeological restoration. In 1979, archaeologists discovered a large number of clay Buddha fragments in the Yongning Temple foundation. These Buddha images, originally enshrined on the pagoda's various levels, were shattered by the fire and thus sealed in the ruins for 1,400 years. One bodhisattva head has a serene expression and gently upturned lips, with gold leaf still glimmering on its clay surface—it is called the "Smile of Yongning Temple," now a treasure of the Luoyang Museum. Standing before this head in the museum display case, and recalling Yang Xuanzhi's account of "fire that burned for three months without going out," you feel a strange sense of time travel—a smile from the ruins is more moving than any intact Buddha image. On the limestone cliffs on both banks of the Yi River in the southern outskirts of Luoyang, where Yongning Temple once stood, lies the world-famous Longmen Grottoes. Just as the Yongning Temple Pagoda was burning down, the large-scale carving of the Longmen Grottoes was just beginning—one wooden pagoda fell, and ten thousand stone Buddhas rose. And fifty kilometers east of Luoyang, in the more tranquil Gong County Grottoes, the "Imperial Procession to Pay Homage to the Buddha" reliefs depict pious Northern Wei imperial family members who may have personally attended the Buddha's birthday ceremonies at Yongning Temple. From wooden pagoda to stone grottoes, from golden bells to carved rock—the Buddhist glory of Northern Wei Luoyang was engraved on paper by Yang Xuanzhi, stroke by stroke.

stops.title: Stop Two: Jingming Temple—The Buddha Light of a Sutra Translation Center
stops.content: According to A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang, Jingming Temple was built by Emperor Xuanwu (Yuan Ke) during the Jingming reign (500–503) and named after the reign era. This temple was unique—not only a place of worship, but also the most important Buddhist scripture translation center of the Northern Wei. Monks from India and the Western Regions translated sutras and preached here, the sound of Sanskrit chanting never ceasing day or night. Yang Xuanzhi wrote: "Of all temples, this one best harmonizes with the mountain's form"—Jingming Temple was perfectly sited, backing onto green mountains and facing flowing water. Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha's birthday, the Buddha images from over a thousand temples in Luoyang were carried out in procession. The Jingming Temple's images were the most exquisite. "Golden flowers shone in the sun, jeweled canopies floated like clouds, banners were as dense as a forest, incense smoke spread like mist"—Yang Xuanzhi's description puts you right in the scene. A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang also records a story about an Indian monk named Bodhiruci who translated sutras at Jingming Temple. The sutras he translated, particularly the Treatise on the Ten Stages, became the theoretical foundation of Northern Wei Buddhism. "On the day of translation, several thousand monks and laypeople gathered." Whenever a new sutra was translated, Luoyang's monks and citizens would swarm in, the scene as intense as the Buddha's birthday procession. Yang Xuanzhi wrote that Bodhiruci lived in the temple for over ten years, and the people of Luoyang respectfully called him "the Tripitaka Master of Translation." The translation hall at Jingming Temple was arguably China's earliest "international academic exchange center"—Indian chanting, Western Region pipa, Central Chinese bells and chimes, all interwoven into a symphony of cultural fusion. Though Jingming Temple has vanished, the Buddhist cultural lineage it carried continues at another temple east of Luoyang that has endured for two thousand years—the White Horse Temple, hailed as "the Origin of Chinese Buddhism." The White Horse Temple is nearly six centuries older than Jingming Temple, being the first officially established Buddhist monastery after Buddhism's introduction to China. Jingming Temple's translation enterprise was the relay and elevation of the "white horse carrying sutras" tradition of the White Horse Temple. From the sutra chests of the White Horse Temple to the translation hall of Jingming Temple, from Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts to Chinese sutra scrolls, Luoyang was always the central stage of Buddhism's Sinicization. Today, green wheat grows on the Jingming Temple site, and farmers till the land where Yang Xuanzhi wrote of "incense smoke spreading like mist." But if you close your eyes and listen to the wind, you may still catch the Sanskrit sounds of Bodhiruci's translation—as Yang Xuanzhi said: "Though the temple is gone, the Dharma is not."

stops.title: Stop Three: Yaoguang Temple—The Serene Beauty of an Imperial Nunnery
stops.content: Yaoguang Temple is a unique temple in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang—an imperial nunnery, located beside the Imperial Avenue beneath the Changhe Gate of the Luoyang palace city, built by Emperor Xiaowen for palace concubines who had become nuns. Yang Xuanzhi records that the temple had "a five-story pagoda, fifty zhang high," with a golden jeweled vase on the spire that could hold twenty-five hu. Even more distinctive was the temple garden—"rare trees and fragrant grasses, beyond description"—it was a rare place of tranquility in the city of Luoyang. The nuns of Yaoguang Temple were mostly women from the Northern Wei imperial harem and noble families. When Yang Xuanzhi wrote of their fate in war, his tone is heavy with grief: "Many of the capital's ladies fell into enemy hands." Yaoguang Temple's rise and fall is the epitome of the Northern Wei dynasty's fate—at its peak, resplendent gold and green; at its fall, destruction without exception. Yang Xuanzhi's description of Yaoguang Temple's garden in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang is exceptionally delicate: "All sorts of rare plants were gathered here." He used the extraordinary vegetation to accentuate the temple's elegance. Even more striking was the golden jeweled vase on the five-story pagoda—"beneath the jeweled vase are thirty tiers of dew-collecting golden plates," a structure identical to Yongning Temple's pagoda, only slightly smaller. In recording these details, Yang Xuanzhi perhaps intended to show posterity that every tall pagoda in Northern Wei Luoyang was the crystallization of the craftsmen's wisdom and faith. The nuns of Yaoguang Temple were not merely ascetics living by lamplight and ancient Buddhas. Many were skilled in music and calligraphy, bringing the cultural refinement of the deep palace into the temple. Empress Dowager Hu herself frequently visited Yaoguang Temple to pay homage—"her carriage came often." This nunnery was once the spiritual sanctuary of Luoyang's elite women. Yang Xuanzhi's brush is especially gentle when writing of Yaoguang Temple, as if he could not bear to disturb the peace of those women who vanished in the turmoil of war. Though Yaoguang Temple has not left a single tile behind, one temple in Luoyang still has its bells ringing after two millennia of Buddhist history—that is the White Horse Temple. The White Horse Temple and Yaoguang Temple—one the beginning of Buddhism's eastward transmission, the other the peak of imperial nunneries; one, the starting point of the white horse carrying sutras, the other, the final resting place of golden branches and jade leaves. From Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han to Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, from Kasyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna to those nameless nuns—within the temples of Luoyang is hidden half the history of Chinese Buddhism.

stops.title: Stop Four: White Horse Temple—The First Temple of Buddhism in China
stops.content: Among all the temples recorded in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang, the White Horse Temple is the most special—it is not just a temple but the very starting point of Buddhism's eastward transmission. Yang Xuanzhi traced the story of Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreaming of a golden figure, sending envoys westward, and the white horse carrying sutras on its return, calling the White Horse Temple "the Origin of Chinese Buddhism." When Yang Xuanzhi revisited Luoyang, the White Horse Temple, though it had also endured warfare, was less damaged because it lay outside the city. He wrote: "The sutra chests in the temple still exist to this day." The sutras carried back from the Western Regions had already been at home in Luoyang for over four hundred years. Today, the White Horse Temple's bells still ring, the story of "the white horse carrying sutras" is carved on stone steles, and the ancient cypresses and curling incense within its grounds make it one of the few temples in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang still thriving with incense. Walking through the White Horse Temple's gate is like opening Yang Xuanzhi's yellowed book—the first sentence begins here. In A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang, Yang Xuanzhi recalled the White Horse Temple's history with a deeply nostalgic touch: "The White Horse Temple was founded by Emperor Ming of the Han." Eight short words carry the full weight of two millennia of Buddhism's eastward journey. He recorded in detail the temple's sutra chests—made of sandalwood, "always offered incense and flowers." In the Eastern Wei period when Yang Xuanzhi revisited Luoyang, though the "crabapple trees before the temple were lush with fruit," the temple had lost the splendor of Emperor Ming's time. Yet it was precisely this "lushness in decline" that deeply moved Yang Xuanzhi—splendor may fade, but faith does not die. Today's White Horse Temple covers about 40,000 square meters. The stone horses before the mountain gate are Song dynasty relics, heads bowed as if bearing a load, just returned from carrying sutras in the Western Regions. The temple's main buildings are arranged along the central axis—Heavenly Kings Hall, Great Buddha Hall, Mahavira Hall, Reception Hall, and Vairocana Pavilion, each ascending. The Yuan-dynasty "dry-lacquer" Buddhas of the Three Ages in the Mahavira Hall are the temple's greatest treasures, their faces solemn yet gentle. Inside the temple grounds stands the Cloud-Equal Pagoda, about thirty-five meters tall, originally built in the Eastern Han and rebuilt in the Jin dynasty, known to the people of Luoyang as "China's First Ancient Pagoda." Compared with those temples in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang that exist only on paper, the White Horse Temple is fortunate—it has endured two millennia of war, earthquakes, and floods, yet always someone has rebuilt it on its ruins. If Yang Xuanzhi knew that his words and this temple had traveled together through two thousand years, he would surely add a happy note under the "White Horse Temple" entry in his Record: "It still stands today, its bells and chimes never cease."

stops.title: Stop Five: Longmen Grottoes—The Wall of a Thousand Buddhas on the Banks of the Yi River
stops.content: Although A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang does not have a chapter directly titled "Longmen Grottoes," Yang Xuanzhi repeatedly mentions Buddhist activities on both banks of the Yi River south of Luoyang. After moving the capital to Luoyang, the Northern Wei imperial court undertook large-scale carving of Buddha niches on the limestone cliffs of the Yi River—this was the origin of the world-famous Longmen Grottoes. In his book, Yang Xuanzhi records that Emperor Xuanwu carved Buddhist caves at Longmen to pray for the blessings of his father, Emperor Xiaowen, and his mother, Empress Dowager Wenzhao—these are the Binyang Cave complex, the largest at Longmen. In the centuries that followed, from the Northern Wei through the Tang, countless emperors, generals, and common people carved niches and statues here, and the cliffs on both banks of the Yi gradually became a giant "wall of a thousand Buddhas." Standing on the banks of the Yi River, gazing up at the seventeen-meter-high Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple—that compassionate yet majestic smile—you will recall Yang Xuanzhi's words from the preface to A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang: "The grief over wheat being harvested is not unique to the ruins of Yin; the lament over millet being gathered is truly felt by the Zhou." The Buddha's smile has crossed a thousand years, while generations of dynasties have passed beneath it. Though Yang Xuanzhi did not devote a separate chapter to Longmen, he refers many times in his Record to the "Yi River stone caves"—what the people of Luoyang called the Longmen Grottoes in that era. He specifically mentions the cave carved by Emperor Xuanwu to pray for his parents—today's Binyang Three Caves. The central Binyang Cave is the largest and most time-consuming Northern Wei cave at Longmen, spanning twenty-four years and mobilizing 800,000 craftsmen. The relief of "The Emperor and Empress Paying Homage to the Buddha" in this cave was stolen and taken overseas in the 1930s, now housed in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art—one of the most heartbreaking pages in Chinese cultural history. The most glorious moment at Longmen came in the Tang dynasty—the Fengxian Temple Vairocana Buddha niche was carved beginning in the third year of the Xianheng reign (672). According to the stele inscription, Empress Wu Zetian "donated 20,000 strings of her cosmetic allowance" for this work. The Buddha is 17.14 meters tall, and its ears alone are 1.9 meters—the face is full and round, eyebrows like crescent moons, eyes slightly downcast, a faint smile at the corners of the mouth. This fusion of "divinity and humanity" is the finest expression of the High Tang spirit. If Yang Xuanzhi could have seen this great Buddha, he would surely have described it in words even more magnificent than "golden flowers shining in the sun." From Longmen, traveling east along the Yi River for about fifty kilometers, there is another Northern Wei imperial grotto—the Gong County Grottoes. Its reliefs of "The Emperor and Empress Paying Homage to the Buddha" are the "sister pieces" to the stolen reliefs from Binyang Cave at Longmen—and perfectly preserved in their original location. The Northern Wei Luoyang Buddhist world of Yang Xuanzhi's writing finds its most direct confirmation in the stones of Longmen and Gong County—words may yellow, stones may weather, but the power of faith transcends all.

stops.title: Stop Six: Gong County Grottoes—The Northern Wei Imperial Procession to Pay Homage to the Buddha
stops.content:
About fifty kilometers east of Luoyang, on the limestone cliffs along the Yi-Luo River in Gongyi, lies a hidden imperial grotto from the same period as the Longmen Grottoes—the Gong County Grottoes. Though Yang Xuanzhi did not write a special entry for it in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang, this grotto was a product of the early Northern Wei imperial Buddhist activities after the capital's relocation to Luoyang.

The Gong County Grottoes have five caves remaining. The most stunning is the relief of "The Emperor and Empress Paying Homage to the Buddha" in the first cave—the most complete surviving Northern Wei imperial Buddhist procession in stone. The emperor, wearing a crown, and the empress, wearing a lotus-flower headdress, are surrounded by attendants, palace ladies, and monks, processing toward the Buddha in a grand, solemn procession. After 1,500 years, the folds of their stone garments still flow, their faces still reverent.

Though the Gong County Grottoes are smaller in scale than Longmen, they preserve a more authentic Northern Wei character. Had Yang Xuanzhi walked this far, he would surely have devoted his brush to this set of reliefs—for they are the most direct stone evidence of the Northern Wei imperial passion for Buddhism that he recorded in A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang.

The Gong County Grottoes consist of five caves, carved beginning in the second year of the Northern Wei Xiping reign (517)—the same year the Yongning Temple Pagoda was built. This chronological coincidence is intriguing: as Empress Dowager Hu erected the tallest wooden pagoda in Luoyang, imperial craftsmen were carving caves on the cliffs along the Yi-Luo River. One of wood, one of stone; one soaring high, one plunging deep—Northern Wei Buddhist faith was engraved into history in two completely different ways. The "Emperor and Empress Paying Homage to the Buddha" in the first cave is arranged in three registers. The emperor wears a crown and imperial robes; the empress wears a lotus headdress; they are surrounded by monks, attendants, palace ladies, and guards—the entire relief is like a frozen imperial Buddhist ceremony.

In A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang, Yang Xuanzhi repeatedly describes the Northern Wei imperial family's Buddhist observances: "Her carriage came often" to Yaoguang Temple, "every year on the fourth day of the fourth month, the Buddha images of all temples go out in procession"... And the relief of paying homage to the Buddha at Gong County Grottoes is the perfect illustration of these words. What the craftsmen carved into stone was not merely the faces of emperors and empresses, but the spiritual portrait of an age—in that war-torn era of the Northern and Southern Dynasties, people poured all their longing for peace into the faces of the Buddhas. The celestial musicians in the caves hold pipa, harps, and panpipes; flowers rain from above, ribbons flutter in the wind—when you gaze at these reliefs in dim lamplight, you can almost hear, as if from a distant time, the "Sanskrit chanting that never ceased day or night" of Yang Xuanzhi's Northern Wei Luoyang.
